summary.text: For every prime \(p\), any admissible integer \(k\le p\) is either \(1\) or is divisible by \(p\), hence must equal \(p\); thus \(a(p)\le 2\). Taking \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\) and arbitrarily large primes \(p>e^4\) gives \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\), contradicting the proposed eventual lower bound.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\#\{k\in\mathbb N:1\le k\le n\text{ and every prime factor of }k\text{ is also a prime factor of }n\}.
\]
We disprove the assertion that for every \(\epsilon>0\) there is an \(N\) such that
\[
(\log n)^{1-\epsilon}\le a(n)
\]
for every \(n\ge N\).

The key observation concerns prime arguments. Let \(p\) be prime. We claim that
\[
a(p)\le 2.
\]
Indeed, the set of prime factors of \(p\) is the singleton \(\{p\}\). Consider any integer \(k\) counted by \(a(p)\). Thus \(1\le k\le p\), and every prime factor of \(k\) belongs to \(\{p\}\).

There are two cases. If \(k=1\), then \(k\) is one of the possible counted integers. If \(k>1\), then \(k\) has at least one prime divisor; call it \(q\). Because all prime factors of \(k\) must be prime factors of \(p\), we have \(q=p\). Hence \(p\mid k\), so \(p\le k\). On the other hand, the defining range for \(a(p)\) gives \(k\le p\). Therefore \(k=p\). Consequently every integer counted by \(a(p)\) lies in \(\{1,p\}\), proving \(a(p)\le 2\). (In fact both \(1\) and \(p\) are counted, so \(a(p)=2\), but only the upper bound is needed.)

Now suppose, for contradiction, that the proposed eventual lower bound is true. Apply it with
\[
\epsilon=\frac12>0.
\]
There would then be a natural number \(N\) such that for every natural number \(n\ge N\),
\[
(\log n)^{1-1/2}=(\log n)^{1/2}\le a(n).
\]

Choose a natural number \(M\) with
\[
M>e^4.
\]
There is a prime \(p\) at least as large as \(\max\{N,M\}\), since primes are unbounded. For completeness, unboundedness follows from Euclid's argument: given any integer bound \(B\), the integer \((B+1)!+1>1\) has a prime divisor \(q\); no prime at most \(B+1\) can divide it, because every such prime divides \((B+1)!\), so \(q>B+1>B\). Thus a prime can always be found beyond any prescribed bound.

Our choice of \(p\) gives both \(p\ge N\) and
\[
p\ge M>e^4.
\]
Since the natural logarithm is strictly increasing on the positive real numbers and \(\log(e^4)=4\), it follows that
\[
\log p>4.
\]
Both sides are positive, so taking square roots preserves the strict inequality. Hence
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}>\sqrt4=2.
\]

On the other hand, because \(p\ge N\), the assumed lower bound at \(n=p\) says
\[
(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p).
\]
Because \(p\) is prime, the observation proved above says
\[
a(p)\le 2.
\]
Combining these inequalities yields
\[
2<(\log p)^{1/2}\le a(p)\le 2,
\]
which is impossible.

Therefore the conjectured statement is false. More explicitly, already for the fixed choice \(\epsilon=\tfrac12\), arbitrarily large primes \(p\) satisfy \(a(p)=2\) while \((\log p)^{1/2}>2\); hence no threshold \(N\) can make the proposed lower bound hold for all \(n\ge N\).
